architectural_implications.after: Deterministic workflow code owns control flow; every LLM call, tool call, and external effect is an activity recorded in event history.
architectural_implications.before: A single process holds conversation/agent state in memory; crashes lose progress or re-trigger paid calls and irreversible tool effects.
architectural_implications.consequence: Replay resumes at the last completed activity; idempotency requirements concentrate at a single, explicit boundary instead of being spread across retry code.
architectural_implications.observation: Orchestration logic and side-effecting tool/LLM calls are currently written as one in-process agent loop.

architectural_implications.after: The execution event history is the source of truth for state and progress.
architectural_implications.before: Engineers design schema for agent state, write retry/reconciliation jobs, and debug divergence between DB state and actual executed effects.
architectural_implications.consequence: Custom state tables and reconciliation jobs disappear, and the same history doubles as an audit trail for regulated review.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent state is conventionally persisted in application-managed tables plus reconciliation jobs.

architectural_implications.after: Approval is delivered as a signal to a durable workflow instance; execution continues when any worker is available.
architectural_implications.before: A worker or container must stay alive (or a cron must poll) for an approval that may arrive hours later.
architectural_implications.consequence: Human latency stops costing compute, and approvals become recorded, replayable events rather than ephemeral application state.
architectural_implications.observation: Human approval is conventionally an in-process await or a polling loop against a DB flag.

architectural_implications.after: Recovery is a runtime primitive; observability is the detection layer feeding an automatic resume path.
architectural_implications.before: Add tracing and dashboards; on failure, an engineer reads traces and manually repairs state.
architectural_implications.consequence: On-call work shifts from manual state repair to monitoring recovery metrics and root-causing recurring activity failures.
architectural_implications.observation: Observability is treated as the answer to agent unreliability.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the reliability KPI from error rate to cost-per-incident and time-to-automatic-resume, using the trust-versus-failure survey split as the diagnostic that the current frame is broken.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders and platform teams running agents in production
article_ideas.based_on: The right reliability target is therefore costless failure, not zero failure
article_ideas.thesis: Reliability engineering for agents has the wrong objective. Chasing zero failures under-invests in the failure path, and the fact that self-described successful teams report 1.7x more continuous issues suggests incident counts measure detection and automation depth rather than quality. The defensible target is costless failure: every crash observable, resumable, and free of duplicate side effects.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Doesn't Need to Stop Failing — It Needs to Fail for Free

article_ideas.angle: Order of operations argument: state design before telemetry design, with the blocker ranking as the evidence that the industry has the order backwards.
article_ideas.audience: SRE, platform, and observability engineers supporting AI systems
article_ideas.based_on: Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery
article_ideas.thesis: Teams respond to agent breakage by adding traces and dashboards, but the top reported blocker is tracking state across services, not seeing failures. Detection and recovery are separate capabilities with separate architectures. If authoritative agent state lives in the execution history rather than an app-managed table, recovery becomes a runtime property and telemetry becomes the trigger for automatic resume instead of a manual repair session.
article_ideas.title: Observability Is Not Recovery: Why Tracing Investment Leaves the #1 Blocker Untouched

article_ideas.angle: Treat the conversion rate as a diagnostic metric, then decompose what breaks in the transition: state, side effects, restart semantics.
article_ideas.audience: Product and engineering managers reporting AI adoption metrics
article_ideas.based_on: There is a persistent ~30-point gap between daily agent usage and production shipping
article_ideas.thesis: Daily agent usage at 80.8% against 49.1% running agents in production is not an adoption lag, it is a capability discontinuity. Prompting a chat assistant and operating an autonomous agent that touches irreversible external effects require different disciplines — idempotency, durable state, replay safety. Track the usage-to-production conversion rate as the leading indicator of infrastructure debt, and stop reading usage growth as production readiness.
article_ideas.title: The 30-Point Gap: Assistant Skills Do Not Transfer to Autonomous Agents

article_ideas.angle: Sell durable execution to the compliance and risk stakeholders rather than to the developer experience budget.
article_ideas.audience: Enterprise architects and risk/compliance stakeholders in financial services
article_ideas.based_on: Enterprise deployment latency is dominated by compliance, auditability, and approvals rather than prototyping capability
article_ideas.thesis: In large regulated organizations, prototype-to-production is not blocked by model capability — 51.3% of teams reach production-ready code in hours while 18.5% of 5,000+ employee firms take months. The delay is approvals, audit trails, and strict error handling. Choosing infrastructure whose execution history is itself the audit record collapses a compliance project into a runtime property, which is a stronger enterprise argument for durable execution than crash recovery.
article_ideas.title: The Audit Trail You Get for Free

connections.relationship: Durable workflow execution is event sourcing applied to process orchestration: recorded events are the authoritative state and are replayed to reconstruct progress.
Moving side-effecting calls behind activities concentrates the idempotency requirement at one explicit interface, which is where retry/dedup semantics must be defined.
Approvals become durable asynchronous events decoupled from process liveness, enabling approval while zero workers run.
The same record used for crash recovery doubles as the audit trail and reproducer required by regulated deployments, collapsing two requirements into one artifact.
Detection and recovery are distinct capabilities; telemetry without resumable state still produces manual 2 AM state repair.

evidence_quotes.text: When workers die and restart, Temporal replays event history so finished LLM calls and activities do not run twice.
Killing worker processes mid-workflow does not lose state or funds.
Demonstrates that durable execution eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs.

core_insights.generalization: Any long-running agent loop that mixes orchestration with irreversible external effects (payments, emails, ticket creation, tool calls) should put effects behind an idempotent activity boundary and make orchestration logic replayable.
core_insights.insight: Durable execution separates deterministic workflow orchestration from side-effecting activities, so on worker crash the runtime replays the event history and resumes without re-executing already-completed LLM calls or activities. The workflow's state is the event log itself, not an app-managed database table.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It removes the entire class of bugs where a restart re-triggers paid LLM calls or duplicate external side effects (e.g., double payouts), which today forces teams to hand-write retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs. Recovery becomes a runtime property rather than application code.

evidence_quotes.text: 85.5% of developers trust agent output at least somewhat (24.7% complete trust, 60.8% somewhat trust).
41.1% of teams hit agent issues daily or more, and 16.4% hit them hourly or more.
Teams that call themselves successful are 1.7x more likely to hit issues continuously.
Failure is inevitable in autonomous agents; engineering must focus on making failures costless rather than aiming for zero failures.

core_insights.generalization: For any autonomous system with non-deterministic components, measure mean cost of recovery per failure and time-to-automatic-recovery rather than only success rate; a higher observed incident count may indicate better detection, not worse system quality.
core_insights.insight: High trust in agent output coexists with very high failure frequency, and the teams that self-report success hit issues more often (1.7x). The right reliability target is therefore costless failure, not zero failure.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It changes the engineering objective from model-quality improvement (reduce error rate) to recovery engineering (make each failure cheap, observable, and self-healing). Teams optimizing for zero failures will under-invest in exactly the mechanism that matters in production.

evidence_quotes.text: 35.7% of teams cite tracking state across services as their #1 blocker.
30.9% cite isolating and debugging issues as #2.
Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery.

core_insights.generalization: In distributed agent systems, the harder engineering problem is durable, resumable state ownership; tracing is necessary but not sufficient, and state design should precede telemetry design.
core_insights.insight: Observability and recoverability are separate capabilities with separate blockers: teams can see that an agent failed but cannot resume it. State tracking across services is the #1 reported blocker, ahead of debugging/tracing.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Investing in traces and dashboards (the default observability response) leaves the dominant blocker — reconstructing and resuming execution state — untouched. The architectural question is where authoritative agent state lives, not how to visualize it.

evidence_quotes.text: Running a payout workflow, stopping the worker process, approving via UI while zero workers are running, and restarting a worker to pick up execution seamlessly.
A 9-stage payout workflow ($2,500 unusual amount) runs locally with an LLM and Temporal.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent workflow with external human or system gating (approvals, escalations, compliance sign-off) should treat the gate as a durable asynchronous signal on a persisted instance rather than an in-process await or a DB-polling loop.
core_insights.insight: Human-in-the-loop approval can be modeled as an external signal to a long-lived durable workflow, so approval can be granted and buffered while zero workers are running, and execution resumes when a worker restarts.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It decouples human latency (hours or days) from process liveness and infrastructure cost: you don't keep a worker or container idling to await approval, and you don't build a polling/persistence scheme yourself. It also gives a natural audit point in the execution history.

evidence_quotes.text: 51.3% of teams go from AI prototype to production-ready code in hours or faster.
In companies with 5,000+ employees, 18.5% say it takes months.
Regulated work (banks, insurers, payments) requires approvals, audit trails, and strict error handling.

core_insights.generalization: For regulated domains, choose infrastructure whose execution record is itself the audit trail and reproducer; otherwise compliance work becomes a bespoke, per-workflow engineering project.
core_insights.insight: Enterprise deployment latency is dominated by compliance, auditability, and approvals rather than prototyping capability: most teams reach production-ready code in hours, but large regulated organizations report months.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It implies the leverage point for enterprise agent adoption is auditable execution history and deterministic replay, which satisfy sign-off requirements as a byproduct, rather than faster prompting or better models.

evidence_quotes.text: 80.8% of users use agents daily or more, up from 47.3% a year prior.
Only 49.1% of teams run agents in production or consider them core to how they ship.
There is a roughly 30% gap between daily usage and production shipping.

core_insights.generalization: Adoption metrics for a new AI capability systematically overstate production readiness; track the usage-to-production conversion rate as a leading indicator of infrastructure gaps.
core_insights.insight: There is a persistent ~30-point gap between daily agent usage and production shipping, meaning assistant-style usage skill does not transfer to operating autonomous agents.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It quantifies that the bottleneck sits at the transition to production (reliability, state, security), not at adoption or experimentation, so engineering budget should be allocated accordingly.

evidence_quotes.text: When workers die and restart, Temporal replays event history so finished LLM calls and activities do not run twice.
Demonstrates that durable execution eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs.

deep_dives.research_question: Which parts of an agent loop must be deterministic for replay to be safe when the branching decisions come from a non-deterministic LLM, and what recording/versioning patterns keep histories compatible across prompt and code changes?
deep_dives.topic: Determinism boundaries in LLM-driven workflow orchestration
deep_dives.trigger_insight: keep agent orchestration code deterministic enough to replay when decisions come from a non-deterministic LLM
deep_dives.why: Replay is only correct if the orchestration code reconstructs the same decision path. The demo replays completed LLM calls as activities, but it does not show how in-workflow branching on model output avoids replay divergence. Without an answer, teams adopting durable execution hit non-determinism errors precisely when they iterate on prompts — the activity they do most.

evidence_quotes.text: Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery.
Failure is inevitable in autonomous agents; engineering must focus on making failures costless rather than aiming for zero failures.
41.1% of teams hit agent issues daily or more, and 16.4% hit them hourly or more.

deep_dives.research_question: Which agent incident classes (worker crash, tool/API failure, poisoned context, wrong model decision) are automatically recovered by event-history replay, and which ones resurface identically after resume?
deep_dives.topic: A taxonomy of failures that replay actually makes costless
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Which failure classes in agent systems are actually made costless by replay
deep_dives.why: The talk asserts failures should be made costless, but replay only guarantees resumption of recorded steps. If the dominant failure mode is a bad reasoning decision, replay faithfully re-executes a workflow that was already wrong. Without a taxonomy, teams will over-attribute reliability to infrastructure and under-invest in detection and rollback at the reasoning layer.

evidence_quotes.text: 35.7% of teams cite tracking state across services as their #1 blocker.
30.9% cite isolating and debugging issues as #2.
Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery.

deep_dives.research_question: Does shifting spend from tracing/dashboards to durable, resumable state ownership reduce manual incident-repair time more than equivalent spend on observability, given that state tracking outranks debugging as a blocker?
deep_dives.topic: State ownership versus telemetry as the primary reliability investment
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Observability and recoverability are separate capabilities with separate blockers
deep_dives.why: The default response to agent unreliability is more traces. The survey says the #1 blocker is tracking state across services, ahead of isolating and debugging issues. If that ordering holds under experiment, most observability roadmaps are aimed at the second-largest problem, and the architectural decision (where authoritative agent state lives) should be made before the telemetry decision.

evidence_quotes.text: Teams that call themselves successful are 1.7x more likely to hit issues continuously.
62% of teams lose measurable time or revenue to AI reliability issues.
Failure is inevitable in autonomous agents; engineering must focus on making failures costless rather than aiming for zero failures.

deep_dives.research_question: What metric set — mean cost per incident, time-to-automatic-resume, duplicate-effect rate — actually discriminates a reliable agent system from an unreliable one better than success rate, and how do these correlate with self-reported team success?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: How should agents be evaluated when the design goal is costless failure rather than zero failure
deep_dives.why: The talk reframes the objective from zero failures to costless failures but supplies no instrument. Teams that self-report success hit issues 1.7x more often, which suggests observed incident counts measure detection sensitivity, not quality. Without replacement metrics, reliability dashboards will keep rewarding the wrong behavior.

evidence_quotes.text: Demonstrates that durable execution eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs.
Killing worker processes mid-workflow does not lose state or funds.

deep_dives.research_question: For a multi-stage, side-effecting agent workflow, what is the measured difference in engineering hours, incident recovery time, duplicate-effect rate, and per-workflow infrastructure overhead between a durable execution runtime and an application-managed state table plus retry and reconciliation jobs?
deep_dives.topic: Comparative cost profile: durable execution versus hand-rolled state tables
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the measurable cost profile of durable execution versus home-grown state tables plus retry logic
deep_dives.why: The central architectural claim of the talk is that durable execution removes state tables, retry logic, and reconciliation jobs. That is a testable engineering-economics claim with no numbers attached. If the runtime overhead per workflow is high and volumes are low, the build-versus-buy conclusion flips for small teams.

project_ideas.name: CrashLoop
project_ideas.poc: Implement the same multi-stage payout workflow twice — once as a durable workflow with side effects behind idempotent activities, once as a single process with a state table and retry logic. Inject SIGKILL at randomized points mid-workflow, restart, and diff the number of executed LLM calls, payouts issued, and workflow completions.

project_ideas.based_on: Human-in-the-loop approval can be modeled as an external signal to a long-lived durable workflow
project_ideas.hypothesis: Modeling human approval as a durable asynchronous signal instead of an in-process await or DB-polling loop drives idle compute during approval wait to zero and reduces approval-wait incident count, at equal or lower total workflow latency.
project_ideas.measurement: Idle compute cost during the approval window, wall-clock time from signal to resumed execution, missed-approval rate, and completeness of the audit record of who approved what and when.
project_ideas.name: SignalGate
project_ideas.poc: Build a 9-stage approval-gated workflow where the gate is a durable signal. Run trials where approval arrives after 1 hour and after 24 hours, with zero workers alive during the wait. Compare against a poller variant and an always-on container variant.

project_ideas.based_on: test replay under code changes and prompt changes to see which mutations break history compatibility
project_ideas.hypothesis: Only workflow mutations that change control flow conditional on model output break replay; recording the LLM decision in history rather than re-deriving it eliminates non-determinism failures across prompt and code changes.
project_ideas.measurement: Replay failure rate per mutation class, percentage of failures attributable to non-recorded decisions, and whether recording decisions restores replay to 100% across the prompt-change axis.
project_ideas.name: Replay Divergence Fuzzer
project_ideas.poc: Take a bug-free durable agent workflow, then systematically mutate it along two axes: (a) prompt/model changes with recorded decisions, (b) control-flow changes that branch on model output. Replay mid-history snapshots after each mutation and record which mutations fail to reconstruct state.

project_ideas.based_on: eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs
project_ideas.hypothesis: Durable execution reduces total cost of ownership versus a hand-rolled state table plus reconciliation jobs once workflows include at least one human-latency gate and one irreversible external effect; below that threshold the reverse holds.
project_ideas.measurement: Engineering hours to first working version, on-call minutes per incident, duplicate-effect incidents per 1,000 runs, and infrastructure cost per 1,000 workflow executions at each volume tier.
project_ideas.name: Durable Bake-off
project_ideas.poc: Build the payout agent both ways, operate both under a synthetic incident load of worker kills, tool timeouts, and delayed approvals, and log engineering hours, remediation minutes, and infrastructure spend per workflow execution across two volume tiers.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Shy Ruparel
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: AI agent reliability, observability, and workflow orchestration using Temporal
  • Purpose: To analyze the state of AI agent adoption in enterprises, expose the reliability and observability gaps, and demonstrate how durable execution platforms like Temporal solve state management, crash recovery, and cost management. Shy Ruparel from Temporal presents findings from the 2026 State of Development survey of 554 engineering leaders using AI agents. The talk examines four major gaps between agent usage and enterprise production: Usage vs. Production, Trust vs. Reality, Prototype vs. Enterprise, and Seeing vs. Recovering. The presentation highlights that while 80.8% of users utilize agents daily, 41.1% hit issues daily or worse, and 62% of teams lose time or revenue to reliability issues. To solve these enterprise reliability and state management blockers, the speaker demonstrates durable execution through a payout workflow demo where state survives worker crashes without rerunning LLM calls or losing audit trails.

Topic Map

Introduction and State of the Agent Survey

  • Explanation: Introduction of the speaker and survey methodology from Temporal's State of Development report (554 engineers and leaders).
  • Key claims:
    • KPMG reported $3T in annual corporate productivity gains from agentic AI in 2025, with financial services leading.
    • 94% of financial services leaders say AI is core to business operations.
    • 62% of teams lose measurable time or revenue to AI reliability issues.
  • Examples:
    • 48.4% of survey respondents have 11+ years of industry experience.
    • Mix of engineers, AI engineers, data engineers, platform teams, and IT leaders (2/3 US, 1/3 UK and EMEA).
  • Terminology:
    • agentic AI
    • durable execution
    • state of development survey
  • Why it matters: Establishes that AI agents are heavily adopted in enterprise finance, but reliability gaps cost teams significant time and revenue.

Gap 1: Usage vs. Production

  • Explanation: Contrasting everyday agent usage frequency with actual production deployment rates.
  • Key claims:
    • 80.8% of users use agents daily or more, up from 47.3% a year prior.
    • Only 49.1% of teams run agents in production or consider them core to how they ship.
    • There is a roughly 30% gap between daily usage and production shipping.
  • Examples:
    • Teams experiment with AI assistants, but something breaks on the way to production.
  • Terminology:
    • usage vs production gap
    • daily agent use
    • production deployment
  • Why it matters: Using an AI assistant is much easier than shipping a reliable autonomous agent into a production environment.

Gap 2: Trust vs. Reality

  • Explanation: Analyzing developer trust in agent outputs compared to how frequently agent systems actually break.
  • Key claims:
    • 85.5% of developers trust agent output at least somewhat (24.7% complete trust, 60.8% somewhat trust).
    • 41.1% of teams hit agent issues daily or more, and 16.4% hit them hourly or more.
    • Teams that call themselves successful are 1.7x more likely to hit issues continuously.
  • Examples:
    • High trust coexists with daily system failures because successful teams look harder for issues.
  • Terminology:
    • trust vs reality
    • issue frequency
    • agent output trust
  • Why it matters: Failure is inevitable in autonomous agents; engineering must focus on making failures costless rather than aiming for zero failures.

Gap 3: Prototype vs. Enterprise

  • Explanation: Comparing the speed of AI prototyping with the slow enterprise deployment timeline.
  • Key claims:
    • 51.3% of teams go from AI prototype to production-ready code in hours or faster.
    • In companies with 5,000+ employees, 18.5% say it takes months.
    • Regulated work (banks, insurers, payments) requires approvals, audit trails, and strict error handling.
  • Examples:
    • Startup speed vs enterprise compliance and auditing requirements.
  • Terminology:
    • prototype vs enterprise
    • startup speed
    • regulated work
  • Why it matters: Enterprise deployment takes months primarily due to compliance, auditability, approvals, and financial safety guarantees.

Gap 4: Seeing vs. Recovering

  • Explanation: The gap between observing that an agent failed and recovering from the failure without manual intervention.
  • Key claims:
    • 35.7% of teams cite tracking state across services as their #1 blocker.
    • 30.9% cite isolating and debugging issues as #2.
    • 22.2% lose progress and redo work because of crashes and restarts.
    • When an agent breaks, the #1 answer for help in surveys was YouTube (47.3%).
  • Examples:
    • Developers reading traces at 2 AM and manually fixing state.
  • Terminology:
    • observability
    • recovery
    • state management
    • event history
  • Why it matters: Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery.

Demo: Payout Workflow with Durable Execution

  • Explanation: A live demonstration of a payout workflow involving an AI agent performing fraud investigation, tool calls, and human-in-the-loop approval.
  • Key claims:
    • A 9-stage payout workflow ($2,500 unusual amount) runs locally with an LLM and Temporal.
    • Killing worker processes mid-workflow does not lose state or funds.
    • When workers die and restart, Temporal replays event history so finished LLM calls and activities do not run twice.
  • Examples:
    • Running a payout workflow, stopping the worker process, approving via UI while zero workers are running, and restarting a worker to pick up execution seamlessly.
  • Terminology:
    • durable execution
    • workflow code
    • activities
    • signals
    • event history
    • replay
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that durable execution eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs.

Key Points

Agent Usage Does Not Equal Production Shipping

  • Explanation: While nearly 81% of survey respondents use agents daily, less than 50% have them running in production or core shipping workflows.
  • Evidence: State of Development survey showing 80.8% daily usage versus 49.1% production deployment.
  • Practical implication: Engineering teams must account for reliability and security infrastructure before claiming agents are production-ready.

High Trust Coexists with High Failure Rates

  • Explanation: 85.5% of developers trust agent output, yet over 41% experience agent issues daily.
  • Evidence: Survey charts showing 85.5% trust vs 41.1% daily issue rate.
  • Practical implication: Teams must plan for failure as a constant reality rather than striving for error-free execution.

State Management is the #1 Enterprise Blocker

  • Explanation: Tracking state across services and debugging distributed agent workflows are the primary productivity bottlenecks for engineering teams.
  • Evidence: 35.7% cited tracking state as the top blocker; 22.2% lose progress from crashes.
  • Practical implication: Investing in durable execution frameworks solves state management without requiring custom database tables or retry code.

Observability vs. Reliability

  • Explanation: Logs and trace tools tell you an agent failed, but durable execution ensures failures cost zero tokens and zero lost progress.
  • Evidence: Comparison of traditional logging (two records drifting apart) vs event history in Temporal (one record for both observability and recovery).
  • Practical implication: Debugging should rely on the execution history rather than separate logs and state databases.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Shy Ruparel
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: AI agent reliability, observability, and workflow orchestration using Temporal
- **Purpose**: To analyze the state of AI agent adoption in enterprises, expose the reliability and observability gaps, and demonstrate how durable execution platforms like Temporal solve state management, crash recovery, and cost management.
Shy Ruparel from Temporal presents findings from the 2026 State of Development survey of 554 engineering leaders using AI agents. The talk examines four major gaps between agent usage and enterprise production: Usage vs. Production, Trust vs. Reality, Prototype vs. Enterprise, and Seeing vs. Recovering. The presentation highlights that while 80.8% of users utilize agents daily, 41.1% hit issues daily or worse, and 62% of teams lose time or revenue to reliability issues. To solve these enterprise reliability and state management blockers, the speaker demonstrates durable execution through a payout workflow demo where state survives worker crashes without rerunning LLM calls or losing audit trails.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and State of the Agent Survey
- **Explanation**: Introduction of the speaker and survey methodology from Temporal's State of Development report (554 engineers and leaders).
- **Key claims**:
  - KPMG reported $3T in annual corporate productivity gains from agentic AI in 2025, with financial services leading.
  - 94% of financial services leaders say AI is core to business operations.
  - 62% of teams lose measurable time or revenue to AI reliability issues.
- **Examples**:
  - 48.4% of survey respondents have 11+ years of industry experience.
  - Mix of engineers, AI engineers, data engineers, platform teams, and IT leaders (2/3 US, 1/3 UK and EMEA).
- **Terminology**:
  - agentic AI
  - durable execution
  - state of development survey
- **Why it matters**: Establishes that AI agents are heavily adopted in enterprise finance, but reliability gaps cost teams significant time and revenue.
### Gap 1: Usage vs. Production
- **Explanation**: Contrasting everyday agent usage frequency with actual production deployment rates.
- **Key claims**:
  - 80.8% of users use agents daily or more, up from 47.3% a year prior.
  - Only 49.1% of teams run agents in production or consider them core to how they ship.
  - There is a roughly 30% gap between daily usage and production shipping.
- **Examples**:
  - Teams experiment with AI assistants, but something breaks on the way to production.
- **Terminology**:
  - usage vs production gap
  - daily agent use
  - production deployment
- **Why it matters**: Using an AI assistant is much easier than shipping a reliable autonomous agent into a production environment.
### Gap 2: Trust vs. Reality
- **Explanation**: Analyzing developer trust in agent outputs compared to how frequently agent systems actually break.
- **Key claims**:
  - 85.5% of developers trust agent output at least somewhat (24.7% complete trust, 60.8% somewhat trust).
  - 41.1% of teams hit agent issues daily or more, and 16.4% hit them hourly or more.
  - Teams that call themselves successful are 1.7x more likely to hit issues continuously.
- **Examples**:
  - High trust coexists with daily system failures because successful teams look harder for issues.
- **Terminology**:
  - trust vs reality
  - issue frequency
  - agent output trust
- **Why it matters**: Failure is inevitable in autonomous agents; engineering must focus on making failures costless rather than aiming for zero failures.
### Gap 3: Prototype vs. Enterprise
- **Explanation**: Comparing the speed of AI prototyping with the slow enterprise deployment timeline.
- **Key claims**:
  - 51.3% of teams go from AI prototype to production-ready code in hours or faster.
  - In companies with 5,000+ employees, 18.5% say it takes months.
  - Regulated work (banks, insurers, payments) requires approvals, audit trails, and strict error handling.
- **Examples**:
  - Startup speed vs enterprise compliance and auditing requirements.
- **Terminology**:
  - prototype vs enterprise
  - startup speed
  - regulated work
- **Why it matters**: Enterprise deployment takes months primarily due to compliance, auditability, approvals, and financial safety guarantees.
### Gap 4: Seeing vs. Recovering
- **Explanation**: The gap between observing that an agent failed and recovering from the failure without manual intervention.
- **Key claims**:
  - 35.7% of teams cite tracking state across services as their #1 blocker.
  - 30.9% cite isolating and debugging issues as #2.
  - 22.2% lose progress and redo work because of crashes and restarts.
  - When an agent breaks, the #1 answer for help in surveys was YouTube (47.3%).
- **Examples**:
  - Developers reading traces at 2 AM and manually fixing state.
- **Terminology**:
  - observability
  - recovery
  - state management
  - event history
- **Why it matters**: Observability tells you an agent failed, but reliability means the failure does not cost you anything or require manual recovery.
### Demo: Payout Workflow with Durable Execution
- **Explanation**: A live demonstration of a payout workflow involving an AI agent performing fraud investigation, tool calls, and human-in-the-loop approval.
- **Key claims**:
  - A 9-stage payout workflow ($2,500 unusual amount) runs locally with an LLM and Temporal.
  - Killing worker processes mid-workflow does not lose state or funds.
  - When workers die and restart, Temporal replays event history so finished LLM calls and activities do not run twice.
- **Examples**:
  - Running a payout workflow, stopping the worker process, approving via UI while zero workers are running, and restarting a worker to pick up execution seamlessly.
- **Terminology**:
  - durable execution
  - workflow code
  - activities
  - signals
  - event history
  - replay
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that durable execution eliminates the need for manual retry logic, state tables, and reconciliation jobs.
## Key Points
### Agent Usage Does Not Equal Production Shipping
- **Explanation**: While nearly 81% of survey respondents use agents daily, less than 50% have them running in production or core shipping workflows.
- **Evidence**: State of Development survey showing 80.8% daily usage versus 49.1% production deployment.
- **Practical implication**: Engineering teams must account for reliability and security infrastructure before claiming agents are production-ready.
